extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, zoologists, and biology students interested in freshwater invertebrates (Hydra and freshwater Polyzoa)
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style morphological and life-history description of Hydra species and freshwater Polyzoa (Ctenostomata & Phylactolæmata), giving diagnostic characters, anatomy, feeding, reproduction, and colony/budding patterns. Useful for identification and comparative taxonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polyzoa taxonomic status
rubrics_metrics.description: The Polyzoa constitute a class in the third great division of the animal kingdom, the so-called Triploblastea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterizing feature: bodies primarily of three cellular layers and usually possessing a body cavity distinct from the alimentary canal. Although heterogeneous, polyzoa share essential features with worms, molluscs, arthropods and vertebrates; the group is nevertheless an isolated one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between zooecium and polypide
rubrics_metrics.description: Most organs fall into two categories connected either with the 'zooecium' (a living cage) or the 'polypide' (organs concerned with nutrition and some musculature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The zooecium is a living envelope secreting an outer covering and has an orifice; when the polypide is retracted part of the zooecium is invaginated forming ectocyst and endocyst structures and a diaphragm. The polypide bears tentacles (lophophore) and alimentary organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lophophore / tentacle characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Tentacles (forming the lophophore) usually surround the mouth in a circle, are covered with cilia in constant motion, are not provided with nettle-cells, and are not highly contractile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They differ from Hydra tentacles in structure and function: they do not seize objects but create currents to waft prey to the mouth; individually capable of motion but usually move in concert; can interlace to prevent escape and may reject unsuitable particles by bending and thrusting them away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Y-shaped alimentary canal anatomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Mouth leads into a funnel-shaped pharynx and oesophagus; the stomach is bulky and glandular with cardiac and pyloric regions; the intestine begins on the ventral side and the alimentary canal is typically Y-shaped with a rectum opening near the mouth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The stomach may have folds (rugæ) and a fundus/caecum; proximal intestine sometimes ciliated. These morphological features vary between polyzoan groups and are important in comparative descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nervous system organization
rubrics_metrics.description: A central ganglion or 'brain' is situated at the base of the tentacles on the side nearest the anus and gives out radiating nerves; an intertentacular organ connects the zooecial cavity with the tentacle cavity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intertentacular organ apparently acts as a passage for genital products, though presence and function may vary seasonally or by condition of the polypide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muscular system components
rubrics_metrics.description: Three important muscle sets: (i) retractor muscles (pull lophophore into zooecium), (ii) parieto-vaginal muscles (connect invaginated portion to main wall), and (iii) parietal muscles (compress the zooecium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parietal muscles are not developed in the Phylactolæmata; descriptions of musculature are diagnostic and should be recorded when comparing taxa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funicular tissue and connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Between polypide and zooecium a reticulate 'funicular' tissue occurs, often concentrated into hollow strands (funiculi) that connect the outer wall of the alimentary canal with the endocyst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The funiculus is important in development of reproductive bodies (e.g., statoblasts) and in connecting new polypide buds with older structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colony formation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The great majority of polyzoa form permanent colonies (polyparia) composed of individual zooecia and polypides connected by living tissue; colonies are formed by budding, not by independent individuals associating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: Entoprocta can show mature solitary individuals; some compound colonies arise by separate colonies secreting a common investment without organic connection. Budding pattern (linear vs cross) is taxonomically informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeding mechanism standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Tentacles do not themselves seize prey but waft it by ciliary currents to the mouth; cilia in the pharynx sweep food in, and tentacles can interlace to prevent escape and reject unsuitable particles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If water contains noxious substances the lophophore is retracted; phylactolæmata possess an epistome capable of closing the mouth completely, acting as an additional safeguard against injurious ingestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gizzard presence and function
rubrics_metrics.description: Some forms possess a 'gizzard' between oesophagus and stomach, but its role varies: in Bowerbankia it is a crushing organ lined with horny projections; in Hislopia or Victorella it serves as an antechamber preserving food or retaining indigestible particles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence, structure, and function of a gizzard are diagnostic characters to note in species descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digestion and excretion pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Digestion mainly occurs in the glandular stomach; excreta are formed into oval masses in the rectum and extruded via the anus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gross indigestible parts are passed per anum, but soluble waste products may be handled by the formation of 'brown bodies' (see Brown bodies criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brown body formation as waste/elimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Degenerating tentacles, alimentary canal and nervous system compact into a rounded 'brown body' (named for its colour); the young polypide-bud forms and may be connected to the brown body by a funiculus, after which the brown body breaks up and its fragments pass into the stomach and out via the anus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brown bodies are common in many colonial polyzoa (rare in phylactolæmata) and are linked to replacement of polypides; they may be pale in some genera (e.g., Hislopia). The extruded collar-like membrane and thickened ectocyst may be associated external signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproductive modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Polyzoa reproduce by (i) eggs, (ii) budding, and (iii) asexually produced dormant bodies (statoblasts) capable of surviving unfavourable conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most species are hermaphrodite with reproductive organs on the inner endocyst surface; fertilization mechanisms may vary and eggs may be fixed to objects or remain attached until cellular layers form. Budding patterns and statoblast production are taxonomically informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budding pattern distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: In freshwater ctenostomes typically three buds are produced from each zooecium (one anterior, two lateral opposite each other) producing a cross arrangement; in phylactolæmata a linear method is typical with granddaughter-buds forming early, producing crowded zooecia and irregular lateral buds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lateral buds may be suppressed producing linear series; Victorella may produce additional adventitious buds. Spontaneous fission of the whole zoarium occurs in some groups (e.g., Lophopinæ). Record budding arrangement when classifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statoblast morphology and taxonomic importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Statoblasts are internal buds with thick horny walls sometimes surrounded by a 'swim-ring' (air-filled chambers) and may bear hooked processes; their external form is very important in classification of the phylactolæmata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statoblast origin involves the funiculus; variants (presence/absence of swim-ring, hooks, wall sculpture) should be noted and used in identification and classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: H. oligactis diagnostic character (1) basal column slender
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Even when the gastral cavity is empty, the basal part of the column is distinctly more slender than the upper part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the first diagnostic distinction between H. oligactis and H. vulgaris.

rubrics_metrics.name: H. oligactis diagnostic character (2) tentacle length
rubrics_metrics.description: (2) Even when the animal is at rest, the tentacles are much longer than the column.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful field/collection character for distinguishing from H. vulgaris.

rubrics_metrics.name: H. oligactis diagnostic character (3) nettle-cell size/shape
rubrics_metrics.description: (3) The nettle-cells of both types are usually smaller and more uniform in size than in the other species; those with barbed threads are always flask-shaped and somewhat narrower in proportion to their length, while those with simple threads are pointed or almost pointed at their distal end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Microscopic characters of nematocysts/nettle-cells are diagnostic; note shape and relative proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: H. oligactis diagnostic character (4) stinging-thread morphology
rubrics_metrics.description: (4) The stinging threads of the more complex form are comparatively stout and short.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morphology of discharged threads (length/stoutness) can help differentiate species/forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: H. oligactis diagnostic character (5) column nettle-cell density
rubrics_metrics.description: (5) There are comparatively few nettle-cells in the column.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relative abundance of nematocysts in column tissue is a diagnostic metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: H. oligactis diagnostic character (6) egg-shell sculpture
rubrics_metrics.description: (6) The egg-shell is nearly smooth or covered more or less completely with short, simple spines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Egg-shell surface sculpture (smooth vs spined) is diagnostic; figure references provided in text (fig. 28, p. 137).

rubrics_metrics.name: H. oligactis form A (large) characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Form A is of vigorous growth, as a rule dioecious, reproductive organs borne practically at any level on the column surface, and eggs spherical and usually covered almost uniformly with spines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form A regarded as forma typica; breeding season noted for N. America (October–December). Egg fixation behavior: eggs fixed to extraneous object by parent, column contracts to place eggs in favourable position.

rubrics_metrics.name: H. oligactis form B (small) characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Form B is smaller, has smaller and more variable nettle-cells, reproductive organs borne only on the distal third or at the base of the column, often monoecious, and the lower surface of its egg flattened, adherent, and devoid of spines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form B breeding season (N. America) September–October; eggs of form B remain attached to the parent until two cellular layers have formed and then drop off. Distinguish from form A when reproductive structures are found.
